notes.title: JOY OF PROGRAMMING 1.0
notes.content:
After one exciting year in Early Access, I am very pleased (and a little proud) to announce the [b]1.0 release of JOY OF PROGRAMMING[/b] and the conclusion of its Early Access phase. This does not mean 1.0 will be the final update. On the contrary: I plan to support JOY OF PROGRAMMING for the foreseeable future and add new levels whenever I have ideas for new challenges. Of course, I also hope the 1.0 release will bring in some new players and our little [url=https://discord.com/invite/2ZrdzkNeBP]community[/url] will grow with more user made levels (check out the level editor after you're comfortable with the game itself)!

I think it is more important than ever to deepen and widen your programming skills, and game-based learning is great opportunity to do just that.

Happy Coding!

Full changelog over the last year until today:
[code]version 1.0.0
- Added "tinygrad" (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad) to third party modules for deep learning
- Increase virtual RAM upgrades (64->128, 128->256, 256->1024)
- Added new machine: VacuumRobot, automatically cleans up all objects with tag "Dirt".
- Added two new Machine Learning levels: Image Classification and Coin Detection
- Added two new Smart Home Levels: VacuumRobot0 and VacuumRobot1
- Improved documentation for several machines

version 0.9.0
- Added a new level:
  - SQL Database (Machine Learning category)
- Preparations for 1.0 release
  - Removed "Beta Map" feature.
  - Cleaned up some obsolete UI
- Linux/Proton support: Please use Proton Experimental. All levels (including image processing levels) now work correctly under Proton Experimental (but not under Proton 9.03).
- Known issues:
  - Localization: While the UI and the tutorials are fully localized in different languages, most other levels do not support localization. These are created with the included level editor which does not support easy localization. Unfortunately, this cannot be easily amended and will not change in the upcoming 1.0 release.

  - Clock Synchronization (Smart Home)

notes.title: Announcing my second game Card Coder
notes.content:
Shortly before the upcoming JOY 1.0 release I have a surprise announcement. I have been secretly working on my second game [b]Card Coder[/b] and can finally reveal the Steam page along with a gameplay trailer:

https://store.steampowered.com/app/3355940/Card_Coder/

Card Coder is a card-building roguelike: A novel mix of tactical card battles, inventory management and roguelike deckbuilding, where YOU create custom cards during each run. There is lots more to say, but I'll keep this brief and hope you'll check out Card Coder. Of course I'm available for any questions or suggestions - either directly here, in the [url=https://discord.com/invite/2ZrdzkNeBP]discord server[/url] or over at the Card Coder discussion page.

notes.title: Update #15 and 1.0 Announcement
notes.content:
Update 15 brings JOY OF PROGRAMMING to version 0.9.0. This update is mostly a maintenance patch for the upcoming 1.0 release and the end of Early Access.

[b]JOY OF PROGRAMMING 1.0[/b] will be released on [b]January 18th 2025[/b] and leave Early Access. This is almost exactly one year after the initial Early Access launch in January 2024. A lot has happened since then and I can confidently say that the game is in much better shape today and contains a lot more content. So a big [b]thank you[/b] to every Early Access player and in particular to everyone who has been reporting bugs, making suggestions or helping others in the game's discord channel. 
To manage expectations for the 1.0 release: There is no big surprise or new feature planned. Rather it will be a content update similar to the previous updates, meaning new levels, fixes and improvements. 

Now back to this update! To shorten the wait, this update does include 1 new level that is a little different from what you've seen so far. Hope you'll like it.

Happy Coding!

Full changelog:
[code]
- Added a new level:
  - SQL Database (Machine Learning category)
- Preparations for 1.0 release
  - Removed "Beta Map" feature.
  - Cleaned up some obsolete UI
- Linux/Proton support: Please use Proton Experimental. All levels (including image processing levels) now work correctly under Proton Experimental (but not under Proton 9.03).
- Known issues:
  - Localization: While the UI and the tutorials are fully localized in different languages, most other levels do not support localization. These are created with the included level editor which does not support easy localization. Unfortunately, this cannot be easily amended and will not change in the upcoming 1.0 release.
[/code]

notes.content:
When throwing a ball, where will it land? In the new challenge map you face a similar task:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/69ddca82bd37a91f734d74b695e06686973361d5.gif[/img]

notes.title: The Robot Arm
notes.content:
First, let me thank everyone for a very successful Steam Next Fest. Your support really means a lot. As we are nearing the Early Access release of JOY OF PROGRAMMING (the exact Date in Q1 2024 will be revealed soon), it's time to shorten the wait and show off another programmable device! Today we'll look at a programmable robot arm with inverse kinematics. 
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/1f43bbfcff54dda51712ebc63164dfc33e59a206.jpg[/img]

With the integrated IK system, you do not have to apply torque control to the individual motors of the arm, but rather can use a local coordinate system to directly set the desired position of the arm's grabber. Then you can pick-up most items, move the arm somewhere else and finally drop the item you are a carrying off again.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/0c8bbd3021fe46c21f59a5a40b73cb3a6ad90615.gif[/img]
(Yeah, we don't talk about the clipping)

Using the robot arm is similar to using any other object in JOY OF PROGRAMMING:
[code]
arm = RobotArm.find("arm1")
#set position in local XYZ (forwards, right, up)
arm.set_grabber_location([1,0,1])
sleep(3) # wait to arrive
arm.pickup() # grab item
#change position 
arm.set_grabber_location([-1,0.5,1.5])
sleep(3) # wait to arrive
arm.release() #drop off item
[/code]


Happy Coding!

notes.title: The Movable Platform
notes.content:
It's time to showcase another programmable device! This time we have a general purpose actuator that can move things around:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/9208090a346dda7c3ba71d8fa7775aec734f3060.jpg[/img]

It might not look like much, but this subtle machine opens up a lot of possibilities. It is simply called the MovablePlatform and its purpose is dynamically positioning otherwise stationary machinery. Let's look at the trusty RangeFinder from the last post. It's already quite useful on its own. But on top of the MovablePlatform? You can move and rotate it however you see fit to measure different areas.

You can place any machine on top of the platform - we are ignoring physical plausibility here for convenience - we are within a simulation after all. Combine it with a robot-arm (more on that machine later) for example to create a very agile transporting system. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/96052deec3cca87247026f7e73d1ebdd708e5cf2.gif[/img]

Using the movable platform in Python code follows the conventions of our object-oriented interface:
[code]
platformScan = MovablePlatform.find("platformScanner")
#rotate by 85 degrees around the up axis
platformScan.set_target_rotation(yaw=85)
[/code]

Happy Coding!

notes.title: The Laser Rangefinder
notes.content:
While I'm currently hard at work to polish a demo for JOY OF PROGRAMMING for the upcoming Steam Next Fest, I'd like to introduce another machine you can work with in the game. The laser rangefinder. This device can measure the distance between itself and some target you point it to.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/48e03ef85bc74ef51c0c28554d8b9c50e9a131f5.gif[/img]

In real-life this nifty piece of technology works by sending out a laser pulse in a narrow beam (like a laser pointer) towards a target and then measuring how long it takes for the reflection of this laser pulse to return to the rangefinder. In the game this can be simulated quite cheaply by sending out a singe line trace from the rangefinder and stopping at the first blocking hit. While measuring distance is very useful in many situations, the in-game rangefinder is turning out to be a multi-purpose sensor than can also read [i]tags[/i] attached to the target, like their type, name, etc, the physical size of the target, its current speed or its mass.

Using the rangefinder in Python code is quite straight forward. Like all entities in JOY OF PROGRAMMING it uses an object-oriented interface. So first you need a reference to one of the rangefinders currently in the game. You can find them either by their respective name or by using the "first" function, if there is only one. Then you call one of the member functions to retrieve information about the target, like its distance to the rangefinder.
[code]
rf = RangeFinder.first()
print(rf.get_distance())
[/code]

Happy Coding!

notes.title: Devlog #10
notes.content:
Writing slow code that works is mostly fine. Writing faster code is better. Writing the fastest code ever? Awesome. JOY OF PROGRAMMING is a single-player experience you play at your own pace and for your own learning and satisfaction. Nevertheless, comparing how well your solution works relative to others' can be quite interesting and provide further insights how to improve. 
Once you finish a level within the game, you will see a minimalistic histogram that tells you how the performance of your solutions compares to those of others (anonymously).

You'll see a comparison with different metrics such as processing time, memory usage or lines of code. If you ever played any of the Zachtronics' games (highly recommended as one of the inspirations for this game and particularly the histogram feature) this will be immediately familiar.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/432e5250b56eed4421f7b8dd8ceb906a73dec69f.png[/img][img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/7f86b4b6176de3980318582cb6e4d4c9167f289c.png[/img]

I'm thinking about further ways to refine this feature such as filtering the histogram to a peer group (those with similar programming experience), visualizing joint distributions (e.g., code that minimizes both, space and runtime requirements) and eventually an optional public leaderboard.

As always, Happy Coding.

notes.title: Devlog #6
notes.content:
While JOY OF PROGRAMMING is mostly about automation, sometimes it is nice to retain some control over what our software is doing. The question how humans best interact with computers (called HCI) has been studied for quite some time. From Douglas Engelbart's invention of the computer mouse in 1963 to modern touch screens or AR/VR headsets, we are always trying to have intuitive interfaces between the user and the computer.
Why am I telling you all this? Because I recently implemented an exciting new feature that allows you to create your own graphical user-interfaces (GUIs) within the game! Here is a quick example.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/2dac7063db7ccef199fc433a7952e6364b1ad34d.jpg[/img]

With a mere 5 lines of code (3 of which are boilerplate), we can create a presentable looking GUI to toggle a lamp in this smart home setting.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/340f0d2ce17c1ff4b15b143881aea810a1c21df2.gif[/img]

Shoutout the creators of [url=https://nicegui.io/]NiceGUI[/url], which I integrated here.

This opens up a whole lot of new possibilities around creating custom dashboards, configuration interfaces, data visualizations and more! Let me know what you think, or if you have any questions!

notes.title: Devlog #5
notes.content:
Obviously we all want to write bug-free code that just works. However in practice, even the most senior devs make mistakes and need to debug their code. Now we can all appreciate a well placed [b]print[/b] statement as the most basic way to get a glimpse at the inner workings of our code. However proper debugging is sometimes needed. Similar to most other modern IDEs, the in-game code editor in JOY OF PROGRAMMING now includes a visual debugger. This means you can comfortably place breakpoints on any code line to stop your code at that point.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/71125c0c31d4a6ea51d1a6fe8740473c61246259.gif[/img]

Then you can step through your code line by line and inspect the value of variables at any time. The real-time simulation of your current environment automatically pauses on breakpoints as well.
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/a4a1d955902ab7646423c8aa62e4bc325eb51969.gif[/img]

Happy debugging!

notes.title: Devlog #3
notes.content:
Currently I'm working on a new category of levels based around breaking ciphers and brute-forcing passwords. Here is a sneak preview into one of them.

[h3]What's my PIN again?[/h3]
You forgot the code for your safe (of course it's your safe, you wouldn't want to open someone else's safe, right? Right?). All you remember is it was 3 digits. That's 1000 possible solutions. Easy but not exactly fun to try out all combinations by hand. A simple brute-force script can automate that and open the lock in a couple of seconds (because you are limited in the number of combinations you can enter per second). However, meet the miracle [b]PinHacker[/b] device:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/eaabc134e754c59419aa1d6af291bf205919ca59.gif[/img]

It can tell you if the pin you entered is greater than or less than the true pin. Could you come up with a more efficient search strategy using this information?

[h3]Python Tips and Tricks[/h3]
The seemingly simple "[b]+[/b]" operator has quite a lot of different uses in Python:
[list]
[*] Add numeric values [code]x = 5 +3[/code]
[*] Concatenate strings [code]print("x is: " + str(x))[/code]
[*] Merge lists [code]long_list = [1,2,3] + [4,5,6][/code]
[/list]
This is done using a principle called [url=https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/operator-overloading-in-python/]operator overloading[/url].

[h3]Quiz Time[/h3]
There are many possible solutions to the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2216770/announcements/detail/3680039889496203881]previous quiz[/url]. One way to simplify the code is [spoiler] to drop the len>0 expression. [code]my_name = "max"
my_age = 38
if my_age>=0 and my_name:
    print("hello there")
else:
    print("invalid")[/code][/spoiler]

Now for today's quiz, what's the output of this code (please use the [noparse][spoiler][/noparse] tag for your answer)?
[code]def clamp(x,a,b):
    if x < a:
        return a
    if x > b:
        return b
    return x

a = 15 / 2
a = clamp(a,0,5)
print(a)[/code]

notes.title: Devlog #2
notes.content:
What is arguably the most important part of a programming game? The code editor! Modern programming requires a good IDE and not just a text editor (unless you are a VIM purist). I'm currently hard at work to give you the best possible coding experience in the integrated code editor within JOY OF PROGRAMMING. Here are some of its most useful features.

[h3]The Amazing Code Editor[/h3]
[b]Syntax Highlighting[/b]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/db095bbaad027807bec2edb94d7843a78f2e534a.jpg[/img]
Important keywords, comments, classes, functions and methods are highlighted in different colors. Eventually more color themes or custom themes will be supported.


[b]Autocompletion / Code Hints[/b]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/4300ea5bca8ecb74c497ecba3d0f26840bca9757.gif[/img]
Maybe the most powerful feature of a good IDE is [b]code completion[/b]. Essentially providing a list of possible tokens while you are typing. Using the power of the underlying mypy linter and it's type inference, the code editor provides you with context sensitive completion hints. So for example, if you type a dot "." after a variable pointing to a conveyor belt, you will see all member methods of the conveyor belt class.


[b]Tooltips on Mouse Hover[/b]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/db8253d60b27cdeee698fb598f1b01a88a463126.gif[/img]
Hover the mouse for a split second over a piece of text and a helpful tooltip will pop-up providing information about the data type, usage details and sometimes example code. You can also select text within the tooltip and copy / paste it (Ctrl-C / Ctrl-V).


[b]Other Goodies[/b]
Smaller QoL features of the code editor include undo/redo (Ctrl-Z / Ctrl-Y), changing the font size (Ctrl + mouse-wheel) and focussing entities in the 3D Viewport from the code (right click on the string name of an entity, e.g. "_entityConveyorBelt0".

[h3]Python Tips and Tricks[/h3]
Python supports very flexible [b]truth testing[/b]. If you are coming from other languages you might be used to writing your if conditions like so:
[code]some_list = [5,6,9]
if len(some_list) > 0:
    do_stuff()
[/code]
However Python supports truth testing any object. And by default, any object that reports length 0 is considered "False". So you can simplify the code above:
[code]some_list = [5,6,9]
if some_list:
    do_stuff()
[/code]
For more information have a look at the official [url=https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#truth]Python documentation[/url].

[h3]Quiz Time[/h3]
The solution to the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2216770/announcements/detail/5698775975733862400]previous quiz[/url] is [spoiler]---> [b]8[/b] <---[/spoiler].

The [b]next quiz[/b]. Can you simplify this code?
[code]my_name = "max"
my_age = 38
if my_age>=0 and len(my_name)>0:
    print("hello there")
else:
    print("invalid")
[/code]
Write your solutions in the comments below (consider using the [noparse][spoiler] and [code][/noparse] tags).

notes.title: Devlog #1
notes.content:
Welcome to my [b]first devlog[/b] for JOY OF PROGRAMMING to keep you in the loop with the development of the game. In every devlog, I will briefly highlight [b]one feature of the game[/b] and a short [b]Python snippet or programming trick[/b]. And sometimes I'll leave you with a [b]Python question / quiz[/b] at the end.

[h3]The Trusty Conveyor Belt[/h3]
To kick off this series, who is better suited than the trusty conveyor belt?
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/ee1d218d62332062643df1c4f16b8fa830d47d7c.gif[/img]

It can move stuff forwards and backwards at a variable speed between -5 and +5. It can also tell you if it is transporting something or not.
Neat.
Here is a short example how you take control of the conveyor belt:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43325028/3de3f2b04a47cdc17e68d8942b3e19a6aaef02a4.jpg[/img]

[h3]Python Tips and Tricks[/h3]
Lets say you have a numeric variable [b]a[/b]. Now you want to add 2 to it. Instead of writing [b]a=a+2[/b], you can also write [b]a+=2[/b].
